Surah 94: Al-Sharh (The Expansion)

It is also called Surat al-Sharh. As narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr and Aisha, it is Meccan. Ibn al-Darис, al-Nahhas, al-Bayhaqi and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted this from Ibn Abbas. In another report from him there is an addition: it was revealed after al-Duha. Al-Biqa'i claimed that according to him it is Medinan. In a lengthy hadith transmitted by Ibn Mardawayh from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, there is what is apparent in indicating that His words in it, ﴿So indeed, with hardship comes ease﴾ ﴿Indeed, with hardship comes ease﴾, were revealed in Medina. However, the soundness of the hadith is open to question. Its verses number eight by consensus, and it is very closely connected to Surat al-Duha, to the extent that it is reported from Tawus and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz that they used to say: "They are one surah," and they would recite them in a single rak'ah without separating them with "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful." The Shi'a also hold this view, as al-Tabarsi related from them.

The Imam said: What prompted this view is that His words, ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾, appear to be a continuation of His words, ﴿Did He not find you an orphan?﴾. But this is not so, because the first was at a time when the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was distressed by the harm the disbelievers caused him, and his state was one of trial and constriction of the breast, whereas the second requires that at the time of revelation he was one whose breast was expanded and heart content. How then can these two coincide? There is room for debate here. The truth is that the basis for such matters is transmission (riwayah), not personal opinion (dirayah), and what is established by continuous transmission (mutawatir) is that they are two surahs separated by the basmalah. Yes, they are very closely connected in meaning, and this is indicated by what is in the hadith of the Night Journey, transmitted by Ibn Abi Hatim: "Indeed Allah, exalted is He, said to him, peace and blessings be upon him: 'O Muhammad, did I not find you an orphan and give you shelter, and lost and guide you, and poor and enrich you? And did I not expand your breast, and remove from you your burden, and raise your remembrance? So I am not mentioned except that you are mentioned along with Me.'" The hadith continues.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ Al-sharh (expansion) originally means widening and spaciousness, and its use became common for clarification (idah). From this comes sharaha al-kitab, meaning he clarified the book, because widening and spreading a thing necessarily entails the manifestation of its inner part and what is hidden in it. Likewise it became common for joy of the soul, so that if it were said that it is a customary (urfiyyah) meaning for it, that would not be far-fetched. This is when it is connected to the heart, as one might say: "He expanded his heart with such-and-such," that is, he gladdened it with it, because the heart is like a dwelling for the soul, and widening and enlarging a dwelling customarily entails the joy of its occupant. Likewise when it is connected to the chest, which is the locus of the heart, and this may indicate the broadness of the heart, because the custom is nearly constant that widening what surrounds a dwelling happens when the dwelling is spacious, so what is around it is widened to bring in more delight and the like within it, and thus joy passes indirectly to the soul. It may also mean, when connected to the heart or the chest, an increase in the knowledge within it. It is imagined that these knowledges need a space in which to exist, and that this is their place; therefore when they are many, their place must be wide enough to contain them. It may also mean an increase in what is in the soul of that kind, and it is said likewise: it is imagined that the increase of its knowledges requires its widening, and its widening requires the widening of that to make it like its place. It may also mean the strengthening of the soul with holy power and divine lights, such that it becomes an arena for processions of knowledges, a sky for constellations of attributes, a throne for kinds of manifestations, and a bed for grazing herds of inspirations, so that no affair distracts it from another, and all that is, will be, and has been stands equal before it. The reason for ascribing it to the chest is as already explained, and the sense of "heart" from "chest" and "soul" from "heart" is by the relation of locality and the like, which the soul does not incline to. The intended sense of each of these is determined by the context. The most fitting sense for the context of favour here is the last of these meanings. Others have allowed: the meaning is, did We not make your breast so wide that it encompassed the two worlds of the unseen and the witnessed, and combined the two faculties of receiving and giving, so that the attachment to physical ties did not bar you from drawing in the lights of spiritual faculties, and attachment to the interests of creation did not hinder you from being immersed in the affairs of the Real. It has also been said: the meaning is, did We not relieve your concern and grief by your awareness of the realities of matters and the worthlessness of this world, so that bearing hardships in calling to Allah became easy for you. It is reported from the majority that the meaning is: did We not widen it with wisdom and make it spacious by facilitating for you the reception of what is revealed to you, after it had been hard for you. And from Ibn Abbas and a group: it is an allusion to the splitting of his noble chest in his childhood, peace be upon him. This splitting occurred, according to some reports, with his wet-nurse Halimah. It is reported from her that she said concerning him, peace be upon him: "We did not cease to perceive from Allah, exalted is He, increase and good, until his two years passed and I weaned him, and he grew up with a growth unlike that of boys, and he had not reached two years before he was a sturdy boy. We brought him to his mother, and we were most eager to keep him with us because of the blessing we saw in him. We said to his mother: 'If you would leave him with us until he grows stronger, for we fear for him the plague of Mecca.' So we did not cease with him until she returned him with us, and we went back with him. By Allah, indeed, a month or three after our bringing him back, while he was with his milk-brother behind our tents among our young goats, his brother came running and said: 'That Qurashi brother of mine has been approached by two men in white garments, who threw him down and split open his belly.' So I and his father went running toward him, and we found him standing, his colour drained. His father embraced him and said: 'My son, what is your state?' He said: 'Two men in white garments came to me, threw me down, split open my belly, took something out of it, threw it away, then put it back as it was.' So we returned with him. His father said: 'O Halimah, I fear that my son has been struck. Go and return him to his family before what we dread appears in him.' She said: 'So we carried him to his mother. She said: "Why have you returned him to me? You were eager for him." We said: "We fear disagreement and misfortunes." She said: "That is not the reason. Be truthful with me about your affair." She did not leave us until we told her his story. She said: "Did you fear Satan for him? No, by Allah, Satan has no path over him, and indeed my son has a great destiny. Leave him with you."'"

In a hadith of Abu Ya'la, Abu Nu'aym and Ibn Asakir there is what indicates that this happened to him repeatedly while he was with Halimah. It also occurred to him, peace and blessings be upon him, after his reaching maturity. In al-Durr al-Manthur: Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in the Zawa'id of the Musnad reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that Abu Hurayrah said: "O Messenger of Allah, what was the first thing you saw of the matter of prophethood?" The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, sat up and said: "You have asked, Abu Hurayrah. I was in a desert at twenty years old and some months, when suddenly there was a speech above my head, and a man was saying to another: 'Is it he?' They confronted me with faces I had never seen in any creation, and spirits I had never found in any creature, and garments I had never found on anyone. The two came toward me walking until, when they drew near, each of them took hold of one of my arms, though I could not feel their touch. One of them said to his companion: 'Split his chest open.' One of them then bent down to my chest and split it, as I see it, without blood or pain. He said to him: 'Take out the rancour and envy.' He took out something like a clot, then cast it away. He said to him: 'Put in compassion and mercy.' Then there was something like silver, and then he pierced the big toe of my right foot and said: 'Go forth and be whole.' So I returned going with it, compassion for the young and mercy for the old."

What I have seen in the commentary on al-Hamziyyah by Ibn Hajar al-Makki is the transmission of this report with different wording, and in it: "I was in a wide desert at ten years of age when suddenly there were two men above my head, one of them saying to his companion: 'Is it he?'" To the end of what is in it. So the splitting would be before puberty too, and Allah knows best.

Then, according to both reports, it is not a definitive statement negating that a splitting occurred before it, since it is possible that what gave him the sense of prophethood was this one and not what came before it. It also occurred to him, peace and blessings be upon him, when Gabriel, peace be upon him, came with the revelation in the cave of Hira. Among those who transmitted this are al-Tayalisi and al-Harith in their two Musnads, and likewise Abu Nu'aym, whose wording is: that Gabriel and Michael, peace be upon them both, split his chest and washed it, then said: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾, the verses. It also occurred once more, and the reports have been widely transmitted, contrary to those who denied it, on the night of his Night Journey, peace and blessings be upon him.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i related from Qatadah, who said: Anas ibn Malik narrated to us from Malik ibn Sa'sa'ah, that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "While I was near the House, between sleeping and waking, a basin of gold was brought to me containing Zamzam water, and my chest was opened up to such and such." Qatadah said: I said, meaning to Anas: What do you mean? He said: "To the bottom of my belly." He said: "Then my heart was extracted and washed with Zamzam water, then returned to its place, then filled with faith and wisdom. Then a beast was brought to me, below the mule and above the donkey, the Buraq, and I set off with Gabriel, peace be upon him, until we reached the lowest heaven." To the end of the hadith.

Qadi Abd al-Jabbar objected to this, with the essence being that its occurrence in childhood and before prophethood would entail the precedence of a miracle over prophethood, which is impermissible; and its occurrence after prophethood, although what was mentioned does not follow from it, nonetheless what was mentioned along with it, the hadith of washing and the insertion of compassion and mercy and the filling of faith and wisdom, would be objected to, since washing is something with no effect on spiritual perfection, being rather for the removal of a physical matter, and the insertion of what was mentioned and its filling is not valid, since it is only something God creates in the heart, and it is nothing. But the precedence of a supernatural occurrence over prophethood is permissible in our view, and we call it irhas (preparatory sign). The reports are numerous about its occurrence for him, peace and blessings be upon him, before prophethood. Washing with water was for the removal of a physical matter, and it is not far-fetched that he removed it and washed the place with a particular water such as Zamzam water, as is sound in some reports. For this reason al-Bulqini said that it is superior to the water of al-Kawthar in bringing about a transformation of temperament, and this has a share in spiritual perfection. For this reason the shaykhs direct the travelling seekers among them to the discipline by which the transformation of temperament is attained, and the changes in the states of the soul and its character in youth, maturity and old age point to this.

What is meant by the insertion of compassion and filling with faith, for example, is the insertion of that by which the perfection of that is attained, and the cause is often named by the name of its effect metaphorically; it may also be literal, and the embodiment of meanings is permissible. Al-Arif Ibn Abi Jamrah said, as in al-Mawahib al-Ladunniyyah by al-Asqalani, in essence: what the words of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, indicate of the substantiality and corporeality of the entities among the created things, which the senses have no way to perceive, is as his words, peace and blessings be upon him, indicate in reality itself; and the judgement by the speaker or the like that they are accidental is only in terms of what appeared to him by his intellect, and the intellect is free and stops there. The reality in truth is what is indicated by the report of the Lawgiver, supported by revelation and the holy light, soaring with both wings in the atmosphere of realities to a place where no whisper of the intellect's murmur is heard and no transmitters' "'an'anah" is heard from him. So faith, wisdom and the like are among what the words of the Prophet indicate.

May Allah exalt him and grant him peace (ﷺ) over its substance: the perceptible substances, not meanings, even if whoever reckons it so reckons it thus, the end.

The matter concerning it, whether in belief or in denial, is up to you, and I do not oblige you to believe; for I do not wish to burden you. Some eminent scholars said: Perhaps that belongs to the category of figurative representation (tamthil), since the representation of meanings has occurred often, as he (ﷺ) gave a figurative representation of Paradise and Hellfire on the side of the wall of his noble mosque. Its benefit is the disclosure of the abstract through the perceptible, and it inclines toward its not occurring in reality. Many have said: All that has come concerning the splitting of the chest (sharh al-sadr), the extraction of the heart, and other such matters, must be believed in even if it is contrary to custom (khariq li al-'adah), and its interpretation is not permissible, since power is capable of it. Whoever claims otherwise falls into the abyss of the Mu'tazilah in their interpretation of the texts concerning the questioning by the two angels, the punishment of the grave, the weighing of deeds, the Sirat, and other matters, by whim. As for the wisdom behind that, given that what results from it could be brought about without it, they have spoken at length in explaining it in its proper place. Yes, taking the expansion (sharh) in the verse to mean that is weak according to the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun). And the expression of the affirmation of the expansion through the rhetorical interrogative of its negation is to signal that its affirmation is so evident that no one could answer it with anything other than "Yes." The attribution of the verb to the pronoun of majesty signals His greatness and the elevation of His rank. And the addition of the prepositional phrase, placed between the verb and its object, signals from the outset that the expansion is among the benefits and advantages for him (ﷺ), hastening to bring joy into his noble heart (ﷺ), and arousing his eagerness for what follows it, so that it may settle in him with full settlement at the time of its arrival.

Abu Ja'far al-Mansur read: "Alam nashrah" with a fatha on the ha', and Ibn 'Atiyyah and a group of others explained it as based on the original "Alam nashrahan" with the light emphatic nun, so the nun was changed to an alif and then deleted for lightness, as in the verse:

"Adribu 'anka al-humum tariqaha / darba-ka bi al-sayfi qawnas al-faras"

It is not hidden that the deletion here is weaker than in the verse, since that is in the imperative and this is in negation. For this reason Ibn Jinni in al-Muntaqa related from Abu Mujahid that it is not permissible at all. The emphatic nun is most akin to expansion and elaboration, not brevity and abbreviation. The verse is said to be fabricated (masnu'). The better example for illustration is what Abu Zayd recited in his Nawadir:

"Min ayyi yawmayya mina al-mawti afir / ayawmun lam yuqaddar am yawmun qudir"

Others have said: Perhaps Abu Ja'far made the ha' clear and prolonged it at its point of articulation, so the listener thought he had pronounced it with fatha. In al-Bahr it is stated that this reading has a better explanation than what was mentioned: that the fatha is according to the dialect of some Arabs, in governing with "lam" in the accusative; al-Lihyani related in his Nawadir that among them are those who put "lam" in the accusative and apocopate with "lan," the reverse of what is known among people. On this is the saying of 'A'ishah bint al-A'jam praising al-Mukhtar ibn Abi 'Ubayd:

"Fi kulli ma hamma amda ra'yahu qudumян / wa lam yushawir fi al-amri alladhi fa'ala"

Some explained it as the fatha due to adjacency to what follows, like the kasra in the reading "al-hamdi lillah" with the genitive, and this does not apply to the verse of 'A'ishah, but applies to the others mentioned.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 94, verse 2:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We removed from you your burden﴾ is conjoined (ʿuṭifa) to what was pointed to in the meaning (madlul) of the preceding sentence, as if it were said: "We have expanded your breast for you, and We removed..." etc. "ʿAnka" (from you) is connected to "waḍaʿnā" (We removed), and its placement before the direct object is for the reason previously mentioned: the intention to hasten the joy and to create suspense for what is delayed, and because its description contains a kind of length, so delaying the prepositional phrase after it would undermine the harmony of the parts of the noble composition. The wizr (burden) is the heavy load; i.e., We lifted from you your heavy load.

﴿Who had weighed down your back﴾, that is, made it bear a load that caused it to creak (naqid), which is the sound of something breaking apart and coming loose, namely the cracking. This is not restricted to the sound of pack-animals' saddles or men's bodies. It is also applied to the joints, so one says "the naqid of the joints" and means their sound. Thus the naqid of the back is the sound heard from its joints under the weight of the load. On this is the verse of 'Abbas ibn Mirdas:

"My back creaks from what I have bent beneath of them, though I was compassionate toward them and tender-hearted."

[Page 169]

Attributing the creaking to the load is the attribution of a cause that bears the effect, used figuratively (majaz). The load that weighed down here refers to what proceeded from the Prophet (ﷺ) before the prophethood that he found burdensome to recall, because in his lofty view it was less than what he later attained. Or it refers to his unawareness of the sharia and similar matters that cannot be known except through revelation, together with his seeking them out (ﷺ). Or it refers to his bewilderment (ﷺ) in some matters, such as fulfilling the duty of the message or receiving the revelation. In the early stage of his mission (ﷺ) this weighed on him greatly. Or it refers to what he saw of his people's misguidance, together with his inability to guide them because they did not obey him or submit to the truth. Or it refers to what he saw of their aggression in harming him (ﷺ), or his grief (ﷺ) over the deaths of Abu Talib and Khadijah, on the basis that the surah was revealed after their deaths.

The "laying down" (wad') is understood in the first sense as forgiveness; in the second as removing his heedlessness (ﷺ) about it by teaching him through revelation and the like; in the third as removing what leads to bewilderment; in the fourth as making it easy for him (ﷺ) through practice and habituation; in the fifth as granting some of them guidance to Islam, such as Hamzah, Umar and others; in the sixth as strengthening him (ﷺ) to endure; and in the seventh as removing it by raising him to the heavens, until every angel met him and greeted him, and by his success in beholding his greatest Beloved and his Lord, Mighty and Majestic.

Whatever the case, the statement contains a metaphorical allegory (isti'arah tamthiliyyah), and the "laying down" is a supporting complement (tarshih) for it. There is in it no proof for us regarding infallibility ('ismah), as is not hidden.

Abu Hayyan chose that the laying down of the burden is a metonymy (kinayah) for his (ﷺ) infallibility from sins and his purification from defilements. It is expressed by "laying down" as an exaggeration in the negation of that, as one says: "I have removed from you the hardship of visiting," to one who never visited, as an exaggeration in the negation of visiting from him to him. The allegory on it is in its state, as has been said.

It has been said: the intended meaning is the burden of your community (ummah). It was attributed to him (ﷺ) because of his concern for their affair and his reflection upon their matter. The intended meaning of its laying down is the removal of its peril in this world, namely the immediate punishment, for as long as he (ﷺ) was among them and as long as they sought forgiveness. For He, glorified be He, said: ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them, nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾. But the remoteness of this view is not hidden.

Anas recited "wa-hatatna" and "halalna" in place of "wa-wada'na". Ibn Mas'ud recited: "wa-halalna 'anka wizraka" (and We unloaded from you your burden).

﴿And We raised high your remembrance﴾, through prophethood and other things. And what elevation is like his, that He joined his name, peace be upon him, with His own name, Exalted and Majestic, in the two parts of the testimony of faith; made his obedience to be His obedience; sent blessings upon him among His angels; commanded the believers to send blessings upon him; and addressed him with titles such as ﴿O you wrapped in your cloak﴾, ﴿O you wrapped in your garments﴾, ﴿O Prophet﴾, and ﴿O Messenger﴾. He also mentioned him, glorified is He, in the books of the earlier peoples, and took the covenant from the prophets, peace be upon them, and their nations, that they should believe in him (ﷺ).

It was narrated from Mujahid, Qatadah, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan and others that they said regarding this: "I am not mentioned except that you are mentioned along with me."

There is also a hadith traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ): Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, Ibn Mardawayh, and Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, "from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: 'Jibril, peace be upon him, came to me and said: Your Lord says: Do you know how I have raised your remembrance? I said: Allah knows best. He said: When I am mentioned, you are mentioned along with Me.'"

This mention is among the things confined to what is greater in rank than the mere singling out of the elevation of remembrance, and the great station of his rank is indicated by the words of Hassan:

A radiant one, upon him is the seal of prophethood, a seal from Allah, witnessed, shining and bearing witness.

And Allah joined the name of the Prophet to His own name, when the muezzin says in the five prayers: "I bear witness."

The subtlety of mentioning the elevation after the removal (of burden) is not hidden. The discussion regarding the conjunction and the addition of (لَكَ) is as previously mentioned.

The fa' in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿So indeed, with hardship is ease﴾, according to what is in al-Kashshaf (al-Kashshaf, the commentary of al-Zamakhshari), is a fa' of explanation (fa' fasihah). The statement is a promise to him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, given for consolation and relief.

He said: The polytheists used to reproach the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and the believers for poverty and hardship, until it occurred to his noble mind, upon him be blessings and peace, that they had turned away from Islam because its adherents were poor and despised. So Allah, glorified is He, reminded him of the great blessings He had bestowed upon him. Then, exalted is His majesty, He said: ﴿Indeed, with hardship is ease﴾. It is as if He, glorified is He, had said: We have granted you what We have granted you, so do not despair of the bounty of Allah, the Exalted; for indeed, with the hardship you are in is ease. This clearly indicates that the (al) in "al-'usr" (the hardship) is for a specific reference (al-'ahd). As for the tanwin in "yusran" (ease), it is for magnification (al-taf'im), as if it had been said: Indeed, with hardship is a great ease, and what an ease! The intended meaning is what ease was made available to them of conquests in the days of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, or the ease of the world in general.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 94, verse 6:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, with hardship there is ease﴾ may be a repetition (takrir) of the preceding sentence, to fix its meaning in souls and establish it in hearts, as is the function of repetition. It may also be a new, independent promise (isti'naf), with the alif-lam (of al-'usr) and the tanwin (of yusra) carrying the same sense as before. However, the intended "ease" here is what became available to them in the days of the caliphs, or the ease of the Hereafter. The probability of the independent sentence is the stronger, because of the known superiority of ta'sis (establishing a new meaning) over ta'kid (emphasis). Moreover, the words of God Most High are to be understood in the most eloquent and comprehensive of the two possibilities. The context, as has been stated, is one of consolation and relief, and the independent (isti'naf) construction is grammatical. Its being without the conjunction "wa" (and) is more than can be counted, and there is no need to explain a reason for this, since it is the default.

Isam al-Din said: "It is not far-fetched that the reason for the separation (fasl) is that it takes the form of repetition, so remember this, for it is among the marvels." It has been criticised with something similar to what we have mentioned. The apparent meaning, according to what you have heard regarding the intended "ease," would be to define it (with alif-lam), but it was preferred to make it indefinite for magnification (tafkhim). It may be said that the benefit of the indefinite form is clarity in the sense of ta'sis, because a repeated indefinite noun ordinarily implies difference, and it signals a distinction between hardship and ease.

From what has been mentioned, the reason is also clear for what 'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from al-Hasan, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out happy and joyful, laughing and saying: 'No hardship will overcome two eases. Indeed, with hardship there is ease. Indeed, with hardship there is ease.'"

Some eminent scholars have stated that the sentence confirms what precedes it and is a promise to him (ﷺ) of the facilitation of every difficulty. As for the fa' (the connecting particle), it is said to be causal (sababiyyah), and it has entered upon the cause, though it is customarily used before the effect, because mentioning one of the two calls for mentioning the other. The alif-lam in al-'usr is for comprehensiveness (istighraq), so the cause of revelation is included in it. The tanwin in (yusran) is according to what has preceded, as if it were said: "We have done for you such and such," because with every hardship, such as constriction of the breast, the burden that breaks the back, and obscurity, there is a great ease, such as the expansion of the breast, the lifting of the burden, and the raising of your remembrance. So do not despair of the mercy of God Most High when what grieves you befalls you.

Some others said: the fa' is for deduction (tafri'), and this is of the type of deriving a judgment from evidence in the form of inference from the particular to the universal. That is like your saying: "Do you not see that the human, the horse and the sheep all move the lower jaw when chewing? So know by this that every animal does likewise. Then reflect."

In the second clause, the two aforementioned possibilities also hold, and the independent construction is again the stronger, for the reason already given. On the basis that the hardship is one and the ease is multiple, the result from the two clauses is that with every hardship there are two great eases, and the apparent meaning of these two eases is a worldly ease and an otherworldly ease. It has been said: the apparent meaning is that the second clause is a repetition and an emphasis of the first, so the ease in it is the very same ease as in the first, just as the hardship is the same. The statement is like your saying: "Indeed, with the horseman is a lance; indeed, with the horseman is a lance." This is evident in the unity of the horseman and the lance. "No hardship will overcome two eases" is not a text that requires taking it as independent (isti'naf), since it is valid also on the emphasis reading, by basing it on the tanwin in (yusran) being for magnification. Thus, out of strength of hope, it is understood as the ease of the two abodes, and these are in reality two eases. What supports this is that the second clause does not appear in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, although it is also reported from him: "No hardship will overcome two eases." It has been said: the report may be understood to mean that no single instance of hardship will overcome the mention of ease twice, and its repetition in a context of promise. And this, as you see, is weak.

The well-known view on all these aspects is that the meaning of "with" (ma'a) is a figurative proximity analogous to togetherness, so the word "ma'a" is borrowed to mean "after." This is for the sake of emphasising that ease follows hardship and is closely connected to it. The notion of comprehensiveness has been questioned, since among hardships there are some that are not followed by a worldly ease, such as enduring poverty and sickness until death; and I do not think you would accept the claim that death is a worldly ease, nor that some hardships are not followed by an otherworldly ease either, such as the hardship of the unbeliever. The answer is that the judgment is with respect to believers, as the context of consolation and relief requires, and as is indicated by what Malik transmitted in the Muwatta' from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: Abu 'Ubayda wrote to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with them both), mentioning to him gatherings of the Romans and what he feared from them. 'Umar wrote back to him: "As to what follows: whenever a believing servant is struck by hardship, God Most High will make relief after it, and no hardship will overcome two eases."

This does not resolve the difficulty, for it remains that some hardships of the believer are not followed by a worldly ease, as is evident. Rather, some are not followed by an otherworldly ease either, such as the hardship of the believer who despairs, for he is not rewarded for it in the Hereafter.

The apparent meaning of the otherworldly ease is the reward in the Hereafter for that hardship. The assumption of the patient believer leaves the question that some of his hardship is also not followed by a worldly ease. Some answered on the emphasis reading that the comprehensiveness is customary (curfi), and it suffices that hardship is generally followed by ease. On the independent reading, the answer is the same, together with the stipulation that the judgment concerns the patient believer. Another answer is that the judgment is conditional upon God's will, even though this is not mentioned. It has been said: this is hinted at by what 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Qatada regarding the verse, who said: "It has been mentioned to us that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) gave good news of this verse to his Companions, and said: 'No hardship will overcome two eases, God willing.'"

It is understood from the words of some excellent scholars that on the emphasis reading it is permissible for (ma'a) to be in its literal sense, and the tanwin in (yusran) to be for kind (nau'iyyah). There is no difficulty with comprehensiveness, since a person in a state of hardship is never free of some kind of ease, and the least of it is that what is greater than what has befallen him is averted from him. It is also permissible for the tanwin to be for magnification, and the great ease that accompanies the hardship is the averting of that greater thing, and there is no hardship except that with God Most High there is something greater than it and greater still. This is not contradicted by: "No hardship will overcome two eases," either because the meaning is that no single instance of hardship will overcome the mention of ease twice in a context of consolation, or because the verse has conveyed that with hardship there is ease, and it is known that after it there is another, according to the customary pattern that prevails, or it is understood from His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿God will bring about, after hardship, ease﴾ (65:7), if its revelation was earlier.

Some have said that the literal togetherness (ma'iyyah) is intended among the elite, in the sense that whatever the Beloved does is beloved, as is indicated by the saying of Shaykh 'Umar ibn al-Farid, may his secret be sanctified:

"Your torment is sweet to me, and your tyranny upon me is justice, by what passion decrees for you."

And the saying of another:

"Whatever reaches my soul from You is a place of gratitude; from the arrow it is cruelty, and from the dagger, oppression."

Calling that "hardship" is because it is so in itself and in the eyes of the common people, not in relation to those lovers who are afflicted by it and find it sweet. All of this, as you see, is so. Furthermore, the intended literal togetherness is made remote by what al-Bazzar, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman transmitted from Anas ibn Malik, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was sitting, and in front of him was a hole. He (ﷺ) said: 'If hardship came and entered this hole, ease would come until it entered upon it and brought it out.' Then God Most High sent down: ﴿Indeed, with hardship there is ease﴾, etc." The wording of al-Tabarani is: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: ﴿So indeed, with hardship there is ease﴾."

Taking the verse as referring to a specific known case (al-'ahd) is safer from disputation, and perhaps those who chose it did so for that reason, together with the support it finds in the occasion of revelation. However, what the apparent wording and its discursive contexts require is comprehensiveness. If this is adopted, then it must be restricted by the condition that the one who suffers the hardship is confident in God Most High, of good hope in Him, glorious and mighty, devoted to Him, glory be to Him, or by something similar of these qualifications. So reflect. And God Most High is the Facilitator of everything that is difficult.

Ibn Wathhab, Abu Ja'far and 'Isa read "al-'usur" and "yusuran" in both places with a damma on the sin.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 94, verse 7:

﴿So when you are free﴾, i.e., from an act of worship such as conveying the revelation, ﴿then labour﴾, i.e., exert yourself in another act of worship, in gratitude for what We have counted over to you of the past blessings and promised you of the recent favours. It is as if the Mighty and Majestic, when He enumerated to him what He enumerated and promised him what He promised, moved him, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, by what He promised, to be thankful and to strive diligently in worship, and not to leave any of his times empty of it. So when he finished one act of worship, he followed it with another.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 94, verse 8:

﴿And to your Lord﴾ alone, ﴿turn eagerly﴾ — strive earnestly in asking, and do not ask anyone other than Him, exalted is He, for He is the One able to grant assistance, not any other, mighty and majestic is He.

Ibn Jarir and others narrated through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: that is, when you have ﴿finished﴾ from the prayer, ﴿then toil﴾ in supplication. Something similar is narrated from al-Dahhak and Qatadah. Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud: that is, when you have ﴿finished﴾ from the obligatory duties, ﴿then toil﴾ in the night prayer. From al-Hasan: that is, when you have ﴿finished﴾ from the raid, then strive in worship. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam something similar. Ibn Nasr and a group narrated from Mujahid: that is, when you have finished with the affairs of yourself; and in another wording: from your worldly life (then pray). In another narration from him, something like what was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. The more fitting interpretation of the verse is what has preceded.

As for the statement of Ibn 'Abbas and those with him, it is a restriction of "finishing" and "being occupied" to some acts of worship, either as an example, since the wording is specific and this is the more apparent reading, and the same applies to what was narrated from Ibn Mas'ud; or because prayer is the mother of the bodily acts of worship and supplication is the marrow of worship, so both are indeed so. As for al-Hasan's statement, it has what is widely circulated from the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "We have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad."

This is close, except that it has been objected: the surah is Meccan, and the command to fight came after the Hijrah. Perhaps he holds that it is Medinan, or that this verse is Medinan, or that its ruling was delayed after its revelation, like other verses. Mujahid's statement considers that "finishing" is most often used for being free of worldly occupations, as in the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Seize your leisure before your preoccupation."

This is the weakest of the statements, for it is distant from what the context requires and what the particle "fa" indicates. 'Isam al-Din said: the more fitting is that it means: ﴿So when you have finished﴾ from one ease, ﴿then toil﴾ with another hardship, seeking the two eases. So when you are like that, be eager toward your Lord, meaning: do not bear the hardship of this world hoping for two eases in it, but rather bear the hardship of seeking the Lord and His nearness, exalted is His majesty, for the two eases. End of quote. By my life, this is contrary to what anyone whose mind is sound would understand from the wording.

The verse indicates that what befits the servant's state is that he fill his times with worship, or that he turn to worship after finishing with the affairs of his worldly life, as you have heard in Mujahid's statement concerning it. They mentioned that a man sitting idle without occupation, or busying himself with what does not concern him in his religion or his worldly life, is a result of foolishness of opinion, feebleness of intellect and dominance of heedlessness. From 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "I dislike to see any of you idle and aimless, neither at the work of his worldly life nor at the work of his Hereafter." It is narrated that Shurayk passed by two men wrestling and said: "This is not what the idle person is commanded to do."

Abu al-Sammal read ﴿farighta﴾ with a kasra on the ra', and it is a dialect, but al-Zamakhshari said it is not eloquent. A group read ﴿fanṣab﴾ with a shadda on the ba' and fathah, from al-infisab, and the meaning is: turn fully toward another act of worship. It is attributed to some of the Imamiyya that he read ﴿fanṣib﴾ with a kasra on the sad, and it was said: that is, ﴿when you have finished﴾ from prophethood, ﴿then appoint﴾ 'Ali as the imam. There is no evidence in the verse for the specificity of the object, so the Sunni may take it to mean Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. If the Imami argues with what occurred at Ghadir Khumm, the Sunni denies its indication for what is established with him regarding the appointment, and its soundness according to what the Imami narrates. He argued for what he estimated with the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Order Abu Bakr to lead the people in prayer."

He said: it is more suitable with "when you have finished," since it was issued from him, peace and blessings be upon him, in his final illness before his death (ﷺ), unlike what happened at Ghadir; for it does not show that his time was a finishing from prophethood, just as the appearance that the time of the command is like that does not follow even if it returns. He also said: the meaning is ﴿when you have finished﴾ from the Hajj, ﴿then appoint﴾ 'Ali. This was refuted by the matter of the surah being Meccan, along with what is not hidden.

In al-Kashshaf he said: If that were valid for the Rafidi, it would be valid for the Nasibi to read it thus and make it a command to the appointment, which is the hatred of 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and enmity toward him. There is room for consideration in this. Some people estimated the object as "khalifah" (successor), and the matter there is easy.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this reading is irregular, weak in meaning, and has not been established from any scholar. Zayd ibn 'Ali and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read ﴿fargh-hib﴾ as a command from raghghaba with a shadda on the ghayn, meaning: make the people eager to seek what is with Him, mighty and majestic is He.
